facts.statement: The first fossils of Chirostenotes were a pair of hands discovered in 1914 by George Fryer Sternberg in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: The first fossils of Chirostenotes, a pair of hands, were in 1914 found by George Fryer Sternberg near Little Sandhill Creek in the Campanian Dinosaur Park Formation of Canada

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Chirostenotes is the pair of hands designated CMN 2367.
facts.quote: The holotype is CMN 2367, the pair of hands

facts.statement: Charles Mortram Sternberg named the foot fossils Macrophalangia canadensis in 1932.
facts.quote: In 1932 Charles Mortram Sternberg gave them the name Macrophalangia canadensis

facts.statement: Raymond Sternberg named the lower jaw fossils Caenagnathus collinsi in 1940.
facts.quote: In 1940 he gave them the name Caenagnathus collinsi

facts.statement: Philip J. Currie and Dale Russell linked previously separate hand, foot, and jaw fossils into a single dinosaur in 1988 using a specimen stored since 1923.
facts.quote: In 1988, a specimen from storage since 1923 was discovered and studied by Philip J. Currie and Dale Russell. This fossil helped link the other discoveries into a single dinosaur

facts.statement: Hans-Dieter Sues renamed the species formerly known as Elmisaurus elegans to Chirostenotes elegans in 1997.
facts.quote: In 1997, this was renamed to Chirostenotes elegans by Hans-Dieter Sues

facts.statement: Chirostenotes lived in Alberta, Canada, during the late Cretaceous period approximately 76.5 to 75 million years ago.
facts.quote: Chirostenotes ( ; named from Greek 'narrow-handed') is a genus of oviraptorosaurian dinosaur from the late Cretaceous (about 76.5–75 million years ago) of Alberta, Canada

facts.statement: A 2016 study estimated Chirostenotes to be 2.5 meters long and weigh 100 kilograms.
facts.quote: In 2016 Paul estimated its length at 2.5 m and its weight at 100 kg (220 lbs)

facts.statement: Chirostenotes possessed a beak, long forelimbs with strong claws, slender hind feet, and a crest similar to that of cassowaries.
facts.quote: Chirostenotes se caracterizaba por la presencia de un pico, extremidades superiores largas que presentaban fuertes garras, dedos de la pata delgados y una cresta similar a las de los casuarios

facts.statement: Chirostenotes measured approximately 2.85 meters in length, 90 centimeters high at the hip, and weighed an estimated 50 kilograms.
facts.quote: Chirostenotes medía aproximadamente 2,85 metros de largo y 90 centímetros de alto hasta la cadera, con un peso estimado de 50 kilogramos

facts.statement: Chirostenotes was likely an omnivore or herbivore, inferred from the beaks of related species.
facts.quote: Chirostenotes was probably an omnivore or herbivore, based on evidence from the beaks of related species like Anzu wyliei and Caenagnathus collinsi

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Chirostenotes may have used its unusually straight second claw to impale soft-bodied prey like grubs, unarmored amphibians, reptiles, and mammals.
facts.quote: They suggested that Chirostenotes may have fed on soft-bodied prey that could be impaled by the second claw, such as grubs, as well as unarmored amphibians, reptiles, and mammals

facts.statement: A 2005 study suggested the elongated second finger with its straight claw was an adaptation for probing crevices.
facts.quote: In 2005 Phil Senter and J. Michael Parrish published a study on the hand function of Chirostenotes and found that its elongated second finger with its unusually straight claw may have been an adaptation to crevice probing

facts.statement: A 2005 study by Phil Senter and J. Michael Parrish found that the elongated second finger with its unusually straight claw may have been adapted for probing crevices.
facts.quote: En 2005 Phil Senter y J. Michael Parrish publicaron un estudio sobre la función de la mano de Chirostenotes y descubrieron que su segundo dedo alargado con su garra inusualmente recta puede haber sido una adaptación al sondaje de grietas

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Chirostenotes could have fed on soft-bodied prey like larvae, amphibians, reptiles, and unarmored mammals by impaling them with its second claw.
facts.quote: Sugirieron que Chirostenotes podría haberse alimentado de presas de cuerpo blando que podrían ser empaladas por la segunda garra, como larvas, anfibios , reptiles y mamíferos sin armadura

facts.statement: A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and others examined stress fractures and tendon avulsions in theropod dinosaurs to understand their behavior.
facts.quote: En 2001, Bruce Rothschild y otros publicaron un estudio que examina evidencia de fracturas por estrés y avulsiones de tendones en dinosaurios terópodos y las implicaciones para su comportamiento

facts.statement: A study found that only one of the 17 Chirostenotes foot bones examined for stress fractures actually possessed them.
facts.quote: Descubrieron que solo uno de los 17 huesos de los pies de Chirostenotes revisados por fracturas por estrés en realidad los tenía

facts.statement: Macrophalangia canadensis and Caenagnathus sternbergi are listed as synonyms of Chirostenotes.
facts.quote: synonyms: Macrophalangia canadensis Sternberg, 1932 Caenagnathus sternbergi? Cracraft, 1971

facts.statement: Chirostenotes belongs to the family Caenagnathidae.
facts.quote: familia: Caenagnathidae

facts.statement: Chirostenotes is classified within the suborder Oviraptorosauria.
facts.quote: infraordo: Oviraptorosauria

facts.statement: Subsequent studies found that Caenagnathus jaws grouped with traditional caenagnathids but not necessarily with Chirostenotes.
facts.quote: Subsequent studies found that the Caenagnathus jaws did in fact group together with other traditional caenagnathids, but not necessarily Chirostenotes

facts.statement: New specimens described in 2015 and 2020 indicated that Chirostenotes is a distinct form from Caenagnathus.
facts.quote: New specimens described by Funston et al. (2015) and Funston & Currie (2020) indicated that Chirostenotes is a distinct form from Caenagnathus

facts.statement: The first fossils of Chirostenotes, a pair of hands, were found in 1914 by George Fryer Sternberg near Little Sandhill Creek in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Canada.
facts.quote: Los primeros fósiles de Chirostenotes, un par de manos, fueron encontrados en 1914 por George Fryer Sternberg cerca de Little Sandhill Creek en la Formación Dinosaur Park datada del Campaniano de Canadá

facts.statement: In 1924, Charles Whitney Gilmore formally described and named the type species Chirostenotes pergracilis based on notes left by Lawrence Morris Lambe.
facts.quote: En 1924, Charles Whitney Gilmore adoptó el nombre que encontró en las notas de Lambe y describió y nombró a la especie tipo Chirostenotes pergracilis

facts.statement: The generic name Chirostenotes is derived from the Greek words for "hand" and "narrowness".
facts.quote: El nombre genérico se deriva del griego, cheir , "mano", y stenotes , "estrechez"

facts.statement: The holotype specimen for Chirostenotes is NMC 2367, which consists of a pair of hands.
facts.quote: El holotipo es NMC 2367, el par de manos

facts.statement: In 1932, Charles Mortram Sternberg named a set of feet found in Alberta Macrophalangia canadensis.
facts.quote: En 1932 Charles Mortram Sternberg les dio el nombre de Macrophalangia canadensis

facts.statement: In 1936, Raymond Sternberg found a lower jaw specimen (CMN 8776) near Steveville, which he named Caenagnathus collinsi in 1940.
facts.quote: En 1936, su mandíbula inferior, el espécimen CMN 8776, fue encontrada por Raymond Sternberg cerca de Steveville y en 1940 le dio el nombre de Caenagnathus collinsi

facts.statement: In 1988, Philip J. Currie and Dale Russell studied a specimen stored since 1923 that helped link previously separate discoveries into a single dinosaur.
facts.quote: En 1988, un espécimen almacenado desde 1923 fue descubierto y estudiado por Philip J. Currie y Dale Russell

facts.statement: Because Chirostenotes was the first name applied to any of the remains, it was recognized as the only valid name for the animal.
facts.quote: Como el primer nombre aplicado a cualquiera de estos restos fue Chirostenotes, este fue el único nombre que se reconoció como válido

facts.statement: Chirostenotes is the only valid genus name for this animal, despite earlier names like Macrophalangia and Caenagnathus being applied to its parts.
facts.quote: Desde el primer nombre aplicado a cualquier de estos restos fue Chirostenotes, este es el único nombre que es identificado como válido

facts.statement: It is now known that Chirostenotes was a toothless oviraptorosaur, meaning its jaws were originally misidentified and now belong to a different animal, likely a dromaeosaurid.
facts.quote: Ahora que se sabe que Chirostenotes era un ovirraptorosaurio desdentado, las mandíbulas han cambiado de nombre a Richardoestesia y provienen de un dinosaurio desconocido, probablemente un dromeosáurido

facts.statement: Since the late 1980s, most researchers have placed Chirostenotes in its own family, Caenagnathidae.
facts.quote: Desde fines de la década de 1980, la mayoría de los investigadores han colocado al taxón en su propio Caenagnathidae

facts.statement: Chirostenotes lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages, approximately 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Chirostenotes fossils have been found in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: Este dinosaurio, proveniente de la Formación Dinosaur Park, Alberta, Canadá

facts.statement: The discovery of Elmisaurus in 1981, which preserved both hands and feet, supported the hypothesis that Chirostenotes and Macrophalangia were the same animal.
facts.quote: En 1981, el anuncio de Elmisaurus, una forma asiática de la que tanto la mano como los pies habían sido preservados, mostró la solidez de la conjetura de Colbert y Russell

facts.statement: A 2007 cladistic study by Philip Senter cast doubt on whether all large fossils from the Dinosaur Park Formation belonged to the same creature.
facts.quote: En 2007, un estudio cladístico de Philip Senter arrojó dudas sobre la idea de que todos los grandes fósiles de la Formación del Parque de los Dinosaurios pertenecían a la misma criatura

facts.statement: Later studies found that the jaws of Caenagnathus grouped with other traditional caenagnathids but not necessarily with Chirostenotes.
facts.quote: Estudios posteriores encontraron que las mandíbulas de Caenagnathus de hecho se agrupaban junto con otros cenagnátidos tradicionales, pero no necesariamente con Chirostenotes

facts.statement: A 2016 analysis by Funston and Currie found that Elmisaurus belongs within the family Caenagnathidae.
facts.quote: El siguiente cladograma sigue un análisis de Funston & Currie en 2016, que encontró Elmisaurus dentro de Caenagnathidae

facts.statement: In 1997, Hans-Dieter Sues renamed a previously described species as Chirostenotes elegans.
facts.quote: En 1997, este fue renombrado como Chirostenotes elegans por Hans-Dieter Sues

facts.statement: In 2013, the species Chirostenotes elegans was moved to the new genus Leptorhynchos.
facts.quote: La especie se trasladó al nuevo género Leptorhynchos en 2013
